======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Economic liberalisation in India
======================================================================

{{Short description|none}} <!-- "none" is preferred when the title is sufficiently descriptive; see [[WP:SDNONE]] -->
{{Use dmy dates|date=December 2020}}
{{Use Indian English|date=July 2015}}
{{Neoliberalism sidebar}} 
{{Capitalism sidebar}}
{{Liberalism in India|Related}}
'''Economic liberalisation in India''' refers to the policy changes, made mainly from 1991 onwards, that [[open economy|opened]] the [[Economy of India|Indian economy]] to foreign trade and investment and gave markets and private enterprises a larger role.<ref name="originalreport">{{cite report |title=India – Structural Adjustment Credit Project (English) – Presidents report |pages=1 |url=https://documents.worldbank.org/en/publication/documents-reports/documentdetail/999451468260069468/india-structural-adjustment-credit-project |publisher=World Bank |date=12 November 1991 }}</ref><ref name="worldbank">{{cite web |title=Structural adjustments in India – a reportof the Independent Evaluation Group (IEG |url=http://lnweb90.worldbank.org/oed/oeddoclib.nsf/DocUNIDViewForJavaSearch/0586CC45A28A2749852567F5005D8C89 |publisher=World Bank |access-date=30 October 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190509212112/http://lnweb90.worldbank.org/oed/oeddoclib.nsf/DocUNIDViewForJavaSearch/0586CC45A28A2749852567F5005D8C89 |archive-date=9 May 2019 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Although some attempts at liberalisation occurred in 1966 and the early 1980s, a more comprehensive reform came in 1991.

The 1991 reforms followed a [[1991 Indian economic crisis|balance-of-payments crisis]] in which foreign exchange reserves fell to about three weeks of imports. The crisis followed a decade of large [[Government budget balance|fiscal deficits]] and rising [[External debt of India|external debt]], and was triggered by the oil-price spike and the loss of Gulf [[Remittance|remittances]] caused by the [[Gulf War]] of 1990–91, as well as the collapse of trade with the [[Soviet Union]]. The reforms dismantled most industrial licensing, cut tariffs, moved the rupee to a market-determined exchange rate, opened many sectors to foreign investment, and freed interest rates and capital markets.<ref name=":4" /> India borrowed from the [[International Monetary Fund]] (IMF) and the [[World Bank]], whose loans carried policy conditions; how far those conditions, rather than the government's own programme, drove the reforms is disputed. At his now famous budget speech that instituted the reforms, [[Manmohan Singh]] said on 24 July 1991: "Let the whole world hear it loud and clear. India is now wide awake."<ref>{{Cite web |title=Manmohan Singh, India's prime minister from 2004 to 2014, has died |website=[[NPR]] |date=26 December 2024 |url=https://www.npr.org/2024/12/26/1045646076/manmohan-singh-dies-india |last1=Pathak |first1=Sushmita }}</ref> 

Growth has been faster since the reforms than in earlier decades, and poverty has fallen sharply, although economists debate how much of that fall was due to reforms. Critics point to rising income inequality, slow growth in formal employment and agrarian distress, while supporters of the reform argue that land, labour, and agricultural markets were left largely unreformed.<ref name=":12" />

==Pre-liberalisation policies==
{{Further|Economic history of India|Licence Raj}}Indian [[economic policy]] after [[Indian independence movement|independence]] was shaped by the colonial experience, which was exploitative and began as a takeover by a [[East India Company|British trading company]],<ref>{{Cite book |last=Malhotra |first=Aditi |url=https://library.oapen.org/handle/20.500.12657/57067 |title=India in the Indo-Pacific: Understanding India's security orientation towards Southeast and East Asia |date=2022 |publisher=Verlag Barbara Budrich |isbn=978-3-8474-2474-1 |pages=136 |hdl=20.500.12657/57067 |language=English |quote=There was a perpetual fear of foreign influence on the Indian economy. This fear emanated from India’s experience with the East India Company, which had entered the subcontinent as a trading entity in 1757 and later metamorphosed into a colonial power that ruled for almost two centuries.}}</ref> and by leaders' ideas, particularly Prime Minister [[Nehru]]'s exposure to [[Fabian socialism]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Misra |first1=O.P |title=Economic thought of Gandhi and Nehru: a comparative analysis |date=1995 |publisher=MD Publications Pvt. Ltd |location=New Delhi |isbn=978-81-85880-71-6 |page=66 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IxGDqOU03h4C&dq=1995.+Economic+Thought+of+Gandhi+and+Nehru%3A+A+Comparative+Analysis.+M.D.+Publications&pg=PP17}}</ref> Under the [[Indian National Congress|Congress Party]] governments of Nehru and his successors, policy tended toward [[protectionist|protectionism]], with a strong emphasis on [[import substitution industrialization|import substitution industrialisation]] under state monitoring, [[state intervention]] at the micro level in all businesses, especially in labour and [[Financial market|financial markets]], a large [[public sector]], business regulation, and [[central planning]].<ref name="kirit-1">{{cite web|author1=Kelegama, Saman|author2=Parikh, Kirit|title=Political Economy of Growth and Reforms in South Asia|year=2000|version=Second Draft|url=http://www.eldis.org/static/DOC12473.htm|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060211121955/http://www.eldis.org/static/DOC12473.htm|archive-date=11 February 2006}}</ref> The annual growth rate of the [[economy of India|Indian economy]] averaged around 4% from the 1950s to 1980s, while per-capita income growth averaged 1.3%.<ref>{{cite web|date=12 April 2004|title=Redefining The Hindu Rate of Growth|url=http://www.financialexpress.com/news/redefining-the-hindu-rate-of-growth/104268/|work=The Financial Express}}</ref> 

During the brief rule of the [[Janata party|Janata Party]] in the late 1970s, the government, seeking to promote economic self-reliance and indigenous industries, required [[Multinational corporation|multinational corporations]] to partner with Indian corporations. The policy proved controversial, reduced foreign investment, and led to the high-profile exit of corporations such as [[Coca-Cola]] and [[IBM]] from India.<ref name="IMM">{{cite book|title=India: From Midnight To Millennium and Beyond|author=Shashi Tharoor|pages=164–66|publisher=Arcade Publishing|year=2006|isbn=978-1-55970-803-6 }}</ref> They re-entered the Indian market following the reforms.

==Reforms before 1991==

=== 1966 liberalisation attempt ===
In 1966, rapid inflation caused by the [[Sino-Indian War]] and a severe drought forced the Indian government to seek monetary aid from the [[International Monetary Fund|International Monetary Fund (IMF)]] and [[World Bank]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Srinivas|first=V.|date=27 March 2018|title=India's IMF Programmes—1966 and 1981: An Analytical Review|journal=Indian Journal of Public Administration|language=en-US|volume=64|issue=2|pages=219–227|doi=10.1177/0019556117750897|s2cid=188184832|issn=0019-5561}}</ref> Pressure from the{{which|date=November 2025}} [[Bretton Woods system|Bretton Woods]] institutions caused a shift toward economic liberalisation, in which the [[Indian rupee|rupee]] was [[Devaluation|devalued]] to combat inflation (even though devaluation results in increased import costs) and cheapen exports and the former system of tariffs and [[Export subsidy|export subsidies]] was abolished.<ref name=":0">Mukherji, R. (2000). India's Aborted Liberalization-1966. ''Pacific Affairs'', ''73''(3), 377–379. doi:10.2307/2672025</ref> However, a second poor harvest and subsequent industrial recession helped fuel political backlash against liberalisation, characterised by resentment at foreign involvement in the Indian economy and fear that it might signal a broader shift away from socialist policies.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|last1=Bhagwati|first1=Jagdish N.|title=Foreign Trade Regimes and Economic Development: India|last2=Srinivasan|first2=T. N.|publisher=The National Bureau of Economic Research|year=1975|isbn=0-87014-531-2|pages=151–153}}</ref> As a result, trade restrictions were reintroduced, and the Foreign Investments Board was established in 1968 to scrutinise companies investing in India with more than 40% foreign equity participation.<ref name=":0" />

=== Economic reforms during the 1980s ===
[[File:WAP-1_Locomotive_at_Delhi.jpg|thumb|[[Indian locomotive class WAP-1|WAP-1]] locomotive developed in 1980]]
[[File:LIC_Zonal_Office.jpg|thumb|LIC Jeevan Bharti building opened in 1986]]
As it became evident that the Indian economy was lagging behind its East and Southeast Asian neighbours, the governments of [[Indira Gandhi]] and subsequently [[Rajiv Gandhi]] began pursuing economic liberalisation.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book|last=Mohan|first=Rakesh|title=India Transformed: 25 Years of Economic Reforms|publisher=Brookings Institution|year=2018|isbn=9780815736622|pages=68–71}}</ref> The ''New Computer Policy of 1984'' was instrumental, as it eased import restrictions on technology, encouraged private investments, and provided incentives for software exports. This policy led to rapid growth in India's hardware and software sectors. Organizations like NASSCOM (established in 1988) supported the industry by fostering development, standardizing practices, and promoting Indian IT firms globally. India also established Software Technology Parks (STPs) to provide infrastructure, tax benefits, and faster data communications, enabling companies to export software services globally. The governments loosened restrictions on business creation and import controls while also promoting the growth of the automobile, [[Computer Age Management Services|digitalization]], telecommunications and software industries.<ref>History of Computing in India: 1955–2010, Rajaraman, V.</ref>{{page needed|date=July 2020}} These reforms coincided with a rise in average GDP growth from 2.9 percent in the 1970s to 5.6 per cent in the 1980s, although they dismantle the Licence Raj.<ref name=":3" />{{Citation needed|date=January 2022}} Despite Rajiv Gandhi's dream for more systemic reforms, the [[Bofors scandal]] tarnished his government's reputation and impeded his liberalisation efforts.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Bofors prevented Rajiv Gandhi from taking up liberalisation|work=The Economic Times|url=https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/news/politics-and-nation/bofors-prevented-rajiv-gandhi-from-taking-up-liberalisation/articleshow/54814737.cms|access-date=11 September 2020}}</ref>

Growth during the 1980s was higher than in the preceding decades but fragile. It not only culminated in a crisis in June 1991 but also exhibited significantly higher variance than growth in the 1990s. Central to the high growth rate in the 1980s was the high growth of 7.6 percent during 1988–1991.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Panagariya |first=Arvind |date=March 2004 |title=India in the 1980s and 1990s: A Triumph of Reforms |url=https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/wp/2004/wp0443.pdf |website=International Monetary Fund |series=IMF Working Paper WP/04/43}}</ref> Dani Rodrik and Arvind Subramanian attribute the rise in productivity from around 1980 to a "pro-business" shift in government attitudes rather than to market liberalisation.<ref>{{Cite report |url=http://www.nber.org/papers/w10376.pdf |title=From "Hindu Growth" to Productivity Surge: The Mystery of the Indian Growth Transition |last=Rodrik |first=Dani |last2=Subramanian |first2=Arvind |date=2004-03-01 |publisher=National Bureau of Economic Research |doi=10.3386/w10376 |location=Cambridge, MA |language=en}}</ref> [[File:Russia v India income share.png|thumb|Unlike socialist countries like the USSR, India didn't achieve the same level of income equality post-independence.]]

==Liberalisation of 1991==

=== Crisis leading to reforms ===
{{Main|1991 Indian economic crisis}}With the liberalisation of trade in high-value goods like automobiles, electronics, fridges, washing machines, air conditioners, etc., in the 1980s, Indian imports shot up as significant components were imported.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=IMF Working Papers Volume 2004 Issue 043: India in the 1980's and 1990's: A Triumph of Reforms (2004) |url=https://www.elibrary.imf.org/view/journals/001/2004/043/001.2004.issue-043-en.xml |access-date=2024-10-04 |website=IMF eLibrary |doi=10.5089/9781451846355.001 |language=en|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Combined central and state fiscal deficits rose from about 8% of GDP in the first half of the 1980s to 10.1% in the second half, and external debt rose from $20.6 billion in 1980-81 to 64.4 billion in 1989-90.<ref name=":2" /> A study by Valerie Cerra and Sweta Saxena found that real overvaluation of the rupee under the fixed exchange-rate regime, current account deficits and investor confidence all contributed to the 1991 currency crisis.<ref name="IMF">[http://www.uoit.ca/sas/Macroeconomic%20Issues/What1991CrisisIndia.pdf What Caused the 1991 Currency Crisis in India?] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130902172252/http://www.uoit.ca/sas/Macroeconomic%20Issues/What1991CrisisIndia.pdf|date=2 September 2013}}, IMF Staff Papers, Valerie Cerra and Sweta Chaman Saxena.</ref> 

The [[Gulf War|First Gulf War]] in 1991, after the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait, resulted in a huge blow to the Indian economy from a spike in oil prices and a drop in remittances from Indian expats in the Gulf region.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-02-24 |title=Crude above $100: How oil price shocks impacted India's economy in the past |url=https://www.indiatoday.in/diu/story/how-oil-price-shocks-impacted-india-economy-in-the-past-1917380-2022-02-24 |access-date=2024-10-04 |website=India Today |language=en}}</ref> The government was close to default on its external debt<ref name="Ghosh">[http://www.globaleconomicgovernance.org/wp-content/uploads/Ghosh%20-%20India.pdf India's Pathway through Financial Crisis] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111112080531/http://www.globaleconomicgovernance.org/wp-content/uploads/Ghosh%20-%20India.pdf|date=12 November 2011}}. [[Arunabha Ghosh]]. Global Economic Governance Programme. Retrieved 2 March 2007.</ref><ref name="IMF" /> and foreign exchange reserves had fallen to the point that India could barely cover three weeks' worth of imports.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bhattacharya |first=AK |date=2013-01-20 |title=Two months that changed India |url=https://www.business-standard.com/article/beyond-business/two-months-that-changed-india-111070200041_1.html |access-date=2026-10-08 |website=[[Business Standard]]}}</ref>
=== Reforms of 1991 ===
[[File:Visit of Narasimha Rao, Indian Minister for Foreign Affairs, to the CEC (cropped).jpg|thumb|P. V. Narasimha Rao]]
[[File:Manmohansingh04052007.jpg|thumb|Manmohan Singh]]
The collapse of the [[Chandra Shekhar government]] in the midst of the crisis and the [[assassination of Rajiv Gandhi]] led to the election of a new Congress government led by [[P. V. Narasimha Rao]].<ref name=":5">{{Cite book|last=Mohan, Rakesh.|title=India Transformed : Twenty-Five Years of Economic Reforms.|date=2018|publisher=Brookings Institution Press|isbn=978-0-8157-3662-2|location=Washington, DC|pages=44–49|oclc=1056070747}}</ref> He selected Amar Nath Verma to be his Principal Secretary and [[Manmohan Singh]] to be finance minister and gave them complete support in doing whatever they thought was necessary to solve the crisis.<ref name=":5" /> Verma helped draft the New Industrial Policy alongside Chief Economic Advisor [[Rakesh Mohan]], and it laid out a plan to foster Indian industry in five points.<ref name=":4">Verma, A. N. (1991). ''Statement on Industrial Policy'' (India, Ministry of Industry). New Delhi: Government of India.</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Mital|first=Ankit|date=27 August 2016|title=The people behind the Great Men of 1991|url=https://www.livemint.com/Sundayapp/yxBuBRN3kdBr7AO026sHxI/The-people-behind-the-Great-Men-of-1991.html|access-date=6 September 2020|website=Livemint|language=en}}</ref>

* Firstly, it abolished the License Raj by removing licensing restrictions for all industries except for 18 that "related to security and strategic concerns, social reasons, problems related to safety and overriding environmental issues."<ref name=":4" /> 
* To incentivise foreign investment, it laid out a plan to pre-approve all investment up to 51% foreign equity participation, allowing foreign companies to bring modern technology and industrial development.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":4" /> To further incentivise technological advancement, the old policy of government approval for foreign technology agreements was scrapped.
* The fourth point proposed to dismantle public monopolies by floating shares of public sector companies and limiting public sector growth to essential infrastructure, goods and services, mineral exploration, and defense manufacturing.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":4" /> 
* Finally the concept of an MRTP company, where companies whose assets surpassed a certain value were placed under government supervision, was scrapped.<ref name=":5" /><ref>{{Cite web|title=Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act 1970 – GKToday|date=14 September 2011 |url=https://www.gktoday.in/gk/the-monopolies-and-restrictive-trade-practices-act-1970/|access-date=10 September 2020|language=en-US}}</ref>

Meanwhile, Manmohan Singh worked on a new budget that would come to be known as the Epochal Budget.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web|title=Everything about Manmohan Singh's Epochal Budget that marked the beginning of economic liberalisation|url=https://www.freepressjournal.in/webspecial/everything-about-manmohan-singhs-epochal-budget-that-marked-the-beginning-of-economic-liberalisation|access-date=6 September 2020|website=Free Press Journal|language=en}}</ref> The primary concern was getting the fiscal deficit under control, and he sought to do this by [[Austerity|curbing government expenses]]. Part of this was the [[disinvestment]] in public sector companies, but accompanying this was a reduction in subsidies for fertilizer and abolition of subsidies for sugar.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web|date=18 January 2016|title=1991: Economic Reforms|url=https://indiabefore91.in/1991-economic-reforms|access-date=10 September 2020|website=India Before 1991|language=en}}</ref> He also dealt with the depletion of foreign exchange reserves during the crisis with a 19 per cent devaluation of the rupee with respect to the US dollar, a change which sought to make exports cheaper and accordingly provide the necessary foreign exchange reserves.<ref>{{Cite web|date=29 March 2007|title=Devaluation of the Rupee: Tale of Two Years, 1966 and 1991|url=http://www.ccs.in/ccsindia/policy/money/studies/wp0028.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070329195215/http://www.ccs.in/ccsindia/policy/money/studies/wp0028.pdf|archive-date=29 March 2007|access-date=11 September 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | url=http://www.jstor.org/stable/41626979 | jstor=41626979 | title=Rupee Devaluation: Real Issues | last1=Jadhav | first1=N. | journal=Economic and Political Weekly | year=1991 | volume=26 | issue=36 | pages=2119–2120 }}</ref> The devaluation made petroleum more expensive to import, so Singh proposed to lower the price of kerosene to benefit the poorer citizens who depended on it while raising petroleum prices for industry and fuel.<ref>Singh, M. (24 July 1991). ''Budget 1991–1992'' [PDF]. New Delhi: Government of India Ministry of Finance. pp. 11.</ref> Manmohan Singh presented the budget alongside his outline for broader reform.<ref name=":6" /> During the speech he laid out a new trade policy oriented towards promoting exports and removing import controls.<ref name=":8">Singh, M. (24 July 1991). ''Budget 1991–1992'' [PDF]. New Delhi: Government of India Ministry of Finance.</ref> Specifically, he proposed limiting tariff rates to no more than 150 percent while also lowering rates across the board, reducing [[Excise|excise duties]], and abolishing export subsidies.<ref name=":8" />

In August 1991, the [[Reserve Bank of India]] (RBI) Governor established the Narasimham Committee to recommend changes to the financial system.<ref name=GKToday>{{Cite web|title=First Narasimham Committee – GKToday|date=21 April 2011 |url=https://www.gktoday.in/gk/first-narasimham-committee/|access-date=12 September 2020|language=en-US}}</ref> Recommendations included reducing the [[statutory liquidity ratio]] (SLR) and [[cash reserve ratio]] (CRR) from 38.5% and 15% respectively to 25% and 10% respectively, allowing market forces to dictate interest rates instead of the government, placing banks under the sole control of the RBI, and reducing the number of public sector banks.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Akrani|first=Gaurav|title=Narasimham Committee Report 1991 1998 – Recommendations|url=https://kalyan-city.blogspot.com/2010/09/narasimham-committee-report-1991-1998.html|access-date=12 September 2020}}</ref> The government heeded some of these suggestions, including cutting the SLR and CRR rates, liberalizing interest rates, loosening restrictions on private banks, and allowing banks to open branches free from government mandate.<ref name=GKToday/><ref name=":7" />

=== External financing and conditionality ===
On 12 November 1991, based on an application from the Government of India, World Bank sanctioned a structural adjustment loan/credit that consisted of two components – an IBRD loan of $250 million to be paid over 20 years, and an IDA credit of SDR 183.8 million (equivalent to $250 million) with 35 years maturity, through India's ministry of finance, with the President of India as the borrower. The loan was meant primarily to support the government's program of stabilization and economic reform. This specified deregulation, increased foreign direct investment, liberalisation of the trade regime, reforming domestic interest rates, strengthening capital markets (stock exchanges), and initiating public enterprise reform (selling off public enterprises).<ref name="1991wbreport">{{cite web|title=World bank report P-5678-IN – report of the IBRD and IDA on a proposed structural adjustment loan to India|url=http://documents.worldbank.org/curated/en/999451468260069468/pdf/multi0page.pdf|access-date=30 October 2018|publisher=World Bank}}</ref> As part of a bailout deal with the IMF, India was forced to pledge 20 tonnes of gold to [[Union Bank of Switzerland]] and 47 tonnes to the [[Bank of England]] and Bank of Japan.<ref name="reform">[https://www.nytimes.com/1991/06/29/world/economic-crisis-forcing-once-self-reliant-india-to-seek-aid.html Economic Crisis Forcing Once Self-Reliant India to Seek Aid], ''The New York Times'', 29 June 1991</ref>

The reforms drew heavy scrutiny from opposition leaders. The New Industrial Policy and 1991 Budget was decried by opposition leaders as "command budget from the IMF" and worried that withdrawal of subsidies for fertilizers and hikes in oil prices would harm lower and middle-class citizens.<ref name=":6" /> Critics also derided devaluation, fearing it would worsen runaway inflation that would hit the poorest citizens the hardest while doing nothing to fix the trade deficit.<ref>{{cite journal | url=http://www.jstor.org/stable/41498462 | jstor=41498462 | title=Wishful Thinking on Devaluation | journal=Economic and Political Weekly | year=1991 | volume=26 | issue=29 | page=1724 }}</ref> In the face of vocal opposition, the support and political will of the prime minister was crucial in order to see through the reforms.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Balachandran|first=Manu|title=The real architect of India's economic reforms wasn't Manmohan Singh|url=https://qz.com/india/799883/how-narasimha-rao-fixed-the-indian-economy-and-the-congress-party-only-to-be-forgotten/|access-date=6 September 2020|website=Quartz India|date=6 October 2016 |language=en}}</ref> Rao was often referred to as ''[[Chanakya]]'' for his ability to steer tough economic and political legislation through the parliament at a time when he headed a [[minority government]].<ref name="frontline">{{cite journal|author=V. Venkatesan|date=14 January 2005|title=Obituary: A scholar and a politician|url=http://www.hindu.com/thehindu/thscrip/print.pl?file=20050114008013000.htm&date=fl2201/&prd=fline&|journal=Frontline|volume=22|issue=1|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100130013320/http://www.hinduonnet.com/fline/fl2201/stories/20050114008013000.htm|archive-date=30 January 2010|access-date=30 March 2010}}</ref><ref>[http://www.tlca.com/adults/obit-pvn.html PV Narasimha Rao Passes Away]. Retrieved 7 October 2007.  {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071101063203/http://www.tlca.com/adults/obit-pvn.html|date=1 November 2007}}</ref>

=== Compliance Raj after liberalization ===
PM Modi dismantled the [[Planning Commission]] in 2014. Since 2020s, the administration has eliminated over 42,000 unnecessary compliances and decriminalized more than 3,700 legal provisions to enhance the ease of doing business and living.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://morungexpress.com/govt-ended-licence-raj-of-congress-to-usher-in-digital-revolution-pm-modi|title=Govt ended licence raj of Congress to usher in digital revolution: PM Modi|website=MorungExpress}}</ref> In 2022, The government has decided to wind up Tariff Commission, one of the remnants of the licence permit raj, which had outlived its utility.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/articleshow/90631388.cms|title=Govt to shut licence raj era’s Tariff Commission|date=4 April 2022|via=The Economic Times - The Times of India}}</ref>

==Impact==
A 2025 study found that the trade liberalization reduced crony capitalism and productivity loss in India, as politically connected firms lost some of their advantage over other firms.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Jävervall |first1=Sebastian |last2=Khoban |first2=Roza |date=2025 |title=The Impact of Trade Liberalization in the Presence of Political Distortions |url=https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/app.20230629 |journal=American Economic Journal: Applied Economics |language=en |volume=17 |issue=3 |pages=1–41 |doi=10.1257/app.20230629 |issn=1945-7782}}</ref>

=== Credit boom of the 2000s ===
Private investment in infrastructure significantly increased during the 2000s, driven by an influx of global finance.

Reforms in India in the 1990s and 2000s aimed to increase international competitiveness in various sectors, including auto components, [[Telecommunications in India|telecommunications]], [[software]], [[Pharmaceutical industry in India|pharmaceuticals]], [[Biotechnology in India|biotechnology]], [[research and development]], and professional services. These reforms included reducing import tariffs, deregulating markets, and lowering taxes, which led to an increase in foreign investment and high economic growth. From 1992 to 2005, foreign investment increased by 316.9%, and India's GDP grew from $266 billion in 1991 to $2.3 trillion in 2018.<ref>Dutta, M. K. and Sarma, Gopal Kumar, Foreign Direct Investment in India Since 1991: Trends, Challenges and Prospects (1 January 2008).</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Mudgill |first=Amit |title=Since 1991, Budget size grew 19 times, economy 9 times; your income 5 times |work=The Economic Times |url=https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/markets/stocks/news/since-1991-budget-size-grew-19-times-economy-9-times-your-income-5-times/articleshow/62735382.cms?from=mdr#:~:text=At%20$2.3%20trillion,%20the%20Indian,per%20cent%20of%20the%20economy. |access-date=29 August 2020}}</ref>

According to one study, wages rose on the whole, as well as wages as the labor-to-capital [[Wage share|relative share]].<ref name=":9">{{Cite journal |last1=Leblebicioğlu |first1=Asl |last2=Weinberger |first2=Ariel |date=3 December 2020 |title=Openness and factor shares: Is globalization always bad for labor? |url=http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022199620301215 |journal=Journal of International Economics |language=en |volume=128 |article-number=103406 |doi=10.1016/j.jinteco.2020.103406 |issn=0022-1996 |s2cid=229432582|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Extreme poverty reduced from 36 percent in 1993–94 to 24.1 percent in 1999–2000.<ref name=":15">{{Cite web |date=2016-01-18 |title=Impact of reforms |url=https://indiabefore91.in/impact-reforms |access-date=2022-06-15 |website=India Before 1991 |language=en}}</ref>

The liberalisation policies have been criticised for increasing income inequality, concentrating wealth, worsening rural living standards, causing unemployment, and leading to an increase in farmer suicides.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ghosh |first=Jayati |date=2020-12-15 |title=Hindutva, Economic Neoliberalism and the Abuse of Economic Statistics in India |url=https://journals.openedition.org/samaj/6882 |journal=South Asia Multidisciplinary Academic Journal |language=fr |issue=24/25 |doi=10.4000/samaj.6882 |issn=1960-6060 |s2cid=230588392|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=":10" />

India also increasingly integrated its economy with the global economy. The ratio of total [[export]]s of goods and services to GDP in India approximately doubled from 7.3 percent in 1990 to 14 percent in 2000.<ref name="Asiaweek">[http://www.asiaweek.com/asiaweek/96/0412/nat1.html Local industrialists against multinationals]. Ajay Singh and Arjuna Ranawana. ''[[Asiaweek]]''. Retrieved 2 March 2007.</ref> This rise was less dramatic on the import side but was significant, from 9.9 percent in 1990 to 16.6 percent in 2000. Within 10 years, the ratio of total goods and services trade to [[Gross domestic product|GDP]] rose from 17.2 percent to 30.6 percent.<ref name=":15" /> India, however, continues to have a trade deficit, relying on foreign capital to maintain its balance of payments and as such, makes it vulnerable to external shocks.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Singh |first=Sarita Chaganti |date=2023-02-15 |title=India's January merchandise trade deficit hits 1-year low of $17.75 bln |language=en |work=Reuters |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/india/indias-jan-merchandise-trade-deficit-1775-bln-2023-02-15/ |access-date=2023-03-23}}</ref>

Foreign investment in India in form of [[foreign direct investment]], [[portfolio investment]], and investment raised on international capital markets increased significantly, from US$132 million in 1991–92 to $5.3 billion in 1995–96.

However, the liberalization did not benefit all parts of India equally, with urban areas benefiting more than rural areas.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Aghion |first1=Philippe |last2=Burgess |first2=Robin |last3=Redding |first3=Stephen J. |last4=Zilibotti |first4=Fabrizio |year=2008 |title=The Unequal Effects of Liberalization: Evidence from Dismantling the License Raj in India |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/29730127 |journal=The American Economic Review |volume=98 |issue=4 |pages=1397–1412 |doi=10.1257/aer.98.4.1397 |issn=0002-8282 |jstor=29730127 |s2cid=966634}}</ref> States with pro-worker labor laws experienced slower industry expansion compared to those with pro-employer labor laws. This led to a "beggar-thy-neighbor" scenario, where states and cities vie to enact the most pro-capital laws at the expense of workers and other states.

After the reforms, life expectancy and literacy rates continued to increase at roughly the same rate as before the reforms.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.DYN.LE00.IN?locations=IN-CN|title = Life expectancy at birth, total (Years) – India, China &#124; Data}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SE.ADT.LITR.ZS?locations=IN|title = Literacy rate, adult total (% of people ages 15 and above) – India &#124; Data}}</ref> 

By 1997, it became evident that no governing coalition would try to dismantle liberalisation, although governments avoided taking on [[Trade unions in India|trade unions]] and farmers on contentious issues such as reforming labour laws and reducing [[agricultural subsidy|agricultural subsidies]].<ref name="Gandhi-2">{{cite news|date=27 November 1997|title=That old Gandhi magic|newspaper=The Economist|url=http://www.economist.com/world/asia/displaystory.cfm?story_id=107076|access-date=17 January 2011}}</ref> By the turn of the 21st century, India had progressed towards a [[market economy]], with a substantial reduction in state control of the economy and increased financial liberalisation.<ref>{{Harvnb|Kumar|2005|p=1037}}</ref>{{Citation needed|date=January 2021}}

The [[OECD|Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development]] (OECD)<ref>{{Cite web|title=Why open markets matter – OECD|url=https://www.oecd.org/trade/understanding-the-global-trading-system/why-open-markets-matter/|access-date=2022-01-29|website=www.oecd.org}}</ref> applauded the changes, pointing to their promotion of high economic growth and increases in income:

{{blockquote| Its annual growth in [[GDP per capita]] accelerated from just 1¼ per cent in the three decades after Independence to 7½ per cent currently, a rate of growth that will double the average income in a decade.... In service sectors where government regulation has been eased significantly or is less burdensome—such as communications, insurance, asset management and information technology—output has grown rapidly, with exports of [[information technology-enabled services]] particularly strong. In those infrastructure sectors which have been opened to competition, such as [[telecoms]] and [[civil aviation]], the private sector has proven to be extremely effective and growth has been phenomenal.|[[OECD]]<ref name="oecdindia20072">{{cite web|title=Economic survey of India 2007: Policy Brief|url=http://www.oecd.org/dataoecd/17/52/39452196.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110606112149/http://www.oecd.org/dataoecd/17/52/39452196.pdf|archive-date=6 June 2011|publisher=OECD}}</ref>}}

In 2006 India recorded its highest GDP growth rate of 9.6% <ref>{{cite web|title=The World Factbook|url=https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/india/|access-date=10 July 2013|publisher=Cia.gov|archive-date=18 March 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210318202107/https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/india|url-status=dead}}</ref> becoming the second fastest growing major economy in the world, next only to China.<ref name="astaire2">{{cite web|title=The India Report|url=http://www.ukibc.com/ukindia2/files/India60.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090114195859/http://www.ukibc.com/ukindia2/files/India60.pdf|archive-date=14 January 2009|publisher=Astaire Research}}</ref> The growth rate slowed significantly in the first half of 2012.<ref>{{cite news|date=31 May 2012|title=India growth rate slows to 5.3% in first quarter|publisher=BBC|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-18275858|access-date=10 July 2013}}</ref>

The economy then rebounded to 7.3% growth in 2014, 7.9% in 2015 and 8.2% in 2016 before falling to 6.7% in 2017, 6.5% in 2018 and 4% in 2019.<ref>{{Cite web|title=GDP growth (annual %) – India {{!}} Data|url=https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG?locations=IN|access-date=2022-01-29|website=data.worldbank.org}}</ref>

==Later reforms==
{{More citations needed section|date=December 2015}}
During the [[Atal Bihari Vajpayee]] administration, there were extensive liberal reforms, with the [[National Democratic Alliance|NDA Coalition]] beginning the privatisation of government-owned businesses, including hotels, VSNL, Maruti Suzuki, and airports. The coalition also implemented tax reduction policies, enacted fiscal policies aimed at reducing deficits and debts, and increased initiatives for public works.<ref>{{cite web |author=J. Bradford DeLong |year=2001 |title=India Since Independence: An Analytic Growth Narrative |url=http://www.j-bradford-delong.net/Econ_Articles/India/India_Rodrik_DeLong.PDF |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161007103544/http://www.j-bradford-delong.net/Econ_Articles/India/India_Rodrik_DeLong.PDF |archive-date=7 October 2016 |access-date=25 February 2009}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=5 economic decisions by Atal Bihari Vajpayee that changed the face of India |date=16 August 2018 |url=https://www.moneycontrol.com/news/india/5-economic-decisions-by-atal-bihari-vajpayee-that-changed-the-face-of-india-2850581.html |publisher=Moneycontrol}}</ref>

In 2011, the second [[United Progressive Alliance|UPA]] Coalition Government led by [[Manmohan Singh]] proposed the introduction of 51% Foreign Direct Investment in the retail sector. However, the decision was delayed due to pressure from coalition parties and the opposition, and it was ultimately approved in December 2012.<ref>{{cite web|date=14 September 2012|title=End of policy paralysis: Govt approves 51% FDI in multi-brand retail|url=http://zeenews.india.com/business/news/economy/govt-approves-51-fdi-in-multi-brand-retail_60309.html|access-date=10 July 2013|publisher=Zeenews.india.com}}</ref>

After coming to power in 2014, the [[Narendra Modi]] led government launched several initiatives aimed at promoting economic growth and development. One of the notable programs was the "[[Make in India]]" campaign, which sought to encourage domestic and foreign companies to invest in manufacturing and production in India. The program aimed to create employment opportunities and enhance the country's manufacturing capabilities.

=== Privatisation of airports ===
After 2014, the Indian government under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi initiated the privatisation of airports in India as part of its policy of economic liberalisation and development. Under this policy, the Airports Authority of India (AAI) has been engaging in [[Public-Private Partnership]]s (PPP) with private companies for the development, management, and operation of airports in India. This has led to the privatisation of several airports across the country, including those in [[Ahmedabad Airport|Ahmedabad]], [[Chaudhary Charan Singh International Airport|Lucknow]], [[Jaipur International Airport|Jaipur]], [[Guwahati airport|Guwahati]], [[Thiruvananthapuram International Airport|Thiruvananthapuram]], and [[Mangalore International Airport|Mangaluru]].<ref name=":16" />

While the privatisation of airports has been hailed as a step towards modernisation and efficiency, there have also been concerns about the potential impact on workers and the local communities. Critics have argued that the privatisation of airports may lead to job losses and a decline in wages, and that the focus on profit-making may lead to neglect of social and environmental concerns.There have also been controversies around the awarding of contracts to private companies, with allegations of corruption and favouritism in the selection process. However, the government has defended its privatisation policy as a necessary step towards achieving economic growth and development in the country.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2020-11-13 |title='Modi's Rockefeller': Gautam Adani and the concentration of power in India |work=Financial Times |url=https://www.ft.com/content/474706d6-1243-4f1e-b365-891d4c5d528b |access-date=2023-04-23}}</ref>

Under the second NDA Government, the coal industry was opened up through the passing of the Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Bill of 2015. This effectively ended the state monopoly over the mining of the coal sector and opened it up for private, foreign investments, as well as [[private sector]] mining of coal.<ref name=":16">{{cite web|title=Parliament boost to Modi's plans: Coal, mining bills passed by Rajya Sabha|url=http://www.indiatoday.intoday.in/story/rajya-sabha-passes-coal-mining-bill-coal-mines-bill-2015-budget-session-of-parliament/1/424931.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150320133141/http://indiatoday.intoday.in/story/rajya-sabha-passes-coal-mining-bill-coal-mines-bill-2015-budget-session-of-parliament/1/424931.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=20 March 2015|access-date=29 March 2015|publisher=indiatoday.intotoday.in}}</ref>

In the 2016 budget session of Parliament, the [[Narendra Modi]] led NDA Government pushed through the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code to create time-bound processes for insolvency resolution of companies and individuals.<ref>{{cite news|title=Bankruptcy code biggest economic reform after GST: Finance Ministry|newspaper=The Economic Times|url=https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/news/economy/policy/bankruptcy-code-biggest-economic-reform-after-gst-finance-ministry/articleshow/52228931.cms|access-date=11 May 2016}}</ref>

On 1 July 2017, the NDA Government under Modi approved the Goods and Services Tax Act, which had been first proposed 17 years earlier under the NDA Government in 2000. The act aimed to replace multiple indirect taxes with a unified tax structure.<ref>{{cite web|title=F. .No. CBEC-20/05/01/2018-GST Government of India …|url=http://cbic.gov.in/resources//htdocs-cbec/gst/order3-2018-cgst.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180826225922/http://www.cbic.gov.in/resources/htdocs-cbec/gst/order3-2018-cgst.pdf|archive-date=26 August 2018|website=cbic.gov.in|publisher=Ministry of Finance, Government of India}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|date=30 June 2017|title=GST Launch Time Midnight Parliament Session|url=https://www.hindustantimes.com/india-news/gst-launch-times-when-the-parliament-convened-for-a-session-at-midnight/story-c55g94ewrOMefUvQJVFSEO.html|access-date=20 July 2017|work=Hindustan Times}}</ref>

In 2019, Finance Minister [[Nirmala Sitharaman]] announced a reduction in the base corporate tax rate from 30% to 22% for companies that do not seek exemptions, and the tax rate for new manufacturing companies was reduced from 25% to 15%. The Indian government proposed agricultural and labor reforms in 2020, but [[2020–2021 Indian farmers' protest|faced backlash from farmers]] who protested against the proposed agricultural bills. Eventually, due to the sustained protests, the [[2020 Indian agriculture acts|government repealed the agricultural bills]].<ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-05-13|title=Indian lawmakers pass farm bills amid uproar in Parliament|url=https://apnews.com/article/india-legislation-narendra-modi-bills-agriculture-e07f7b1419613cba731560cf3065a9ba|access-date=2022-01-29|website=AP NEWS|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-09-27|title=Explained: In the three new labour codes, what changes for workers & hirers?|url=https://indianexpress.com/article/explained/govts-new-versions-of-labour-codes-key-proposals-and-concerns-6603354/|access-date=2022-01-29|website=The Indian Express|language=en}}</ref>

== Criticisms ==
[[File:Top_10%25_and_bottom_50%25_income_shares_in_India_1900-2021.jpg|thumb|379x379px|Top 10% and bottom 50% income shares in India 1900–2021]]After 1991, the Indian government removed some restrictions on imports of agricultural products causing a price crash while cutting subsidies for the farmers to keep government intervention to the minimum as per neoliberal ideals causing further farmer distress.<ref name=":10" />

The liberalization of the economy made India more vulnerable to global market forces, such as fluctuations in commodity prices, exchange rates and global demand for exports. This increased the country's dependence on global market forces, as it became more susceptible to external shocks and economic crises.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sekhar |first=C. S. C. |date=2004 |title=Agricultural Price Volatility in International and Indian Markets |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/4415712 |journal=Economic and Political Weekly |volume=39 |issue=43 |pages=4729–4736 |issn=0012-9976 |jstor=4415712}}</ref> A commonly cited example of this is the [[2008 financial crisis]]; although the Indian banking sector had low exposure to US banking sector, the crisis still had a negative impact on the Indian economy due to lower global demand, decline in foreign investment and tightening of credit.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.bis.org/publications/paper-54-global-crisis-and-financial-intermediation-emerging-market-economies|title=The global crisis and financial intermediation in emerging market economies|date=24 December 2010|publisher=Bank for International Settlements|via=www.bis.org}}</ref>

=== Employment ===
Initially, the liberalization policies did accelerate the pace of employment generation. However, over the years, this growth in employment has slowed down significantly. A study suggests that even supporters of liberalisation concede that the immediate impact on the labor market has been negative.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Jung |first1=Dong-Hyeon |last2=Choi |first2=Sung-Il |last3=Cho |first3=Jun-Hyeon |last4=Jang |first4=Ji-Yong |date=September 2007 |title=Labour Policy Reform and Labour Market after Economic Liberalization in India |url=http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/223386590701000212 |journal=International Area Review |language=en |volume=10 |issue=2 |pages=193–219 |doi=10.1177/223386590701000212 |s2cid=153649693 |issn=1226-7031|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This is particularly true in sectors like agriculture and manufacturing, where the reforms have not satisfactorily addressed the challenges, resulting in minimal job creation despite high economic growth overall.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Siddiqui |first=Kalim |date=2018 |title=The Political Economy of India's Postplanning Economic Reform: A Critical Review |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.13169/worlrevipoliecon.9.2.0235 |journal=World Review of Political Economy |volume=9 |issue=2 |pages=235–264 |doi=10.13169/worlrevipoliecon.9.2.0235 |jstor=10.13169/worlrevipoliecon.9.2.0235 |issn=2042-891X}}</ref>

The employment growth rate in the period between 2004-2005 and 2011-2012 was just 0.45% per annum, and analyses of long-term trends have indicated that periods of higher economic growth have not translated into job creation, a phenomenon often described as "jobless growth".<ref name=":12">{{Cite journal |last1=Tiwari |first1=Shivakar |last2=Kumar |first2=Surinder |date=2019-06-01 |title=Neo-liberal Macroeconomic Policy and Structural Transformation of Indian Economy: Impact on Income, Employment and Distribution |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s41027-019-00166-9 |journal=The Indian Journal of Labour Economics |language=en |volume=62 |issue=2 |pages=219–238 |doi=10.1007/s41027-019-00166-9 |s2cid=201370554 |issn=0019-5308|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

According to the [[Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy]] (CMIE), although India's population has increased, the workforce has remained stagnant at just over 400 million since 2018 and the quality of jobs has remained low.<ref>{{Cite web |title='India's Workforce Not Rising, Quality of Jobs Very Low': CMIE's Mahesh Vyas |url=https://thewire.in/economy/indias-workforce-not-rising-quality-of-jobs-very-low-cmies-mahesh-vyas |access-date=2024-01-30 |website=The Wire}}</ref>

The service sector, despite its substantial contribution to India's GDP, is often characterized by high productivity but low employment generation. This is because the fastest-growing sub-sectors within services, such as software services, telecommunications, and banking, are capital intensive, not requiring as much labor as other sectors like agriculture or manufacturing. Capital-intensive industries often require the importation of machinery and technology, which can lead to increased current account deficit (with its accompanying vulnerabilities) and is considered a [[Leakage (economics)|leakage]] of domestic investment and spending. India's manufacturing sector has seen increased import intensity, meaning that a significant portion of the inputs needed for production comes from imports.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Service sector: high growth, low employment generation? |url=https://www.businesseconomics.in/service-sector-high-growth-low-employment-generation |access-date=2023-11-06 |website=www.businesseconomics.in}}</ref>

=== Vulnerabilities from international integration ===
The integration into global markets has also made India susceptible to foreign monetary policies, particularly those of the U.S. Federal Reserve. Changes in the Fed's policy rates can have a direct impact on the Indian market through various channels. Rate hikes by the Fed tend to strengthen the U.S. dollar against other currencies, including the Indian rupee, which increases the debt servicing costs for Indian borrowers with loans in foreign currency.

A stronger dollar can lead to capital outflows from India as the interest rate differential between the U.S. and India narrows, making India less attractive to foreign investors as [[emerging market]]s are considered 'risky'. These capital outflows can influence asset prices and increase market volatility in India, as well as deplete foreign exchange reserves and create liquidity issues. India's foreign exchange reserves are built through [[Foreign portfolio investment|foreign capital inflows]] instead of a [[Current account (balance of payments)|current account surplus]] like in the case of Russia or China.

Additionally, the central bank is forced to raise interest rates in order to arrest some of the capital outflows hence reducing domestic demand and accompanying economic effects.

==== Vulnerabilities from global commodity prices ====
India continues to be vulnerable to effects of global commodity prices, particularly the price of crude oil. The long-term effects include a heightened vulnerability to an increase in the import bill and Current Account Deficit, depreciation of the Indian Rupee and an inflationary impact associated with a rise in crude oil prices.<ref name=":14">{{Cite web |last=www.ETEnergyworld.com |title=India's import dependence on crude oil climbs to 87.8% in April-August 2023: PPAC - ET EnergyWorld |url=https://energy.economictimes.indiatimes.com/news/oil-and-gas/indias-import-dependence-on-crude-oil-climbs-to-87-8-in-april-august-2023-ppac/103822860 |access-date=2023-11-06 |website=ETEnergyworld.com |language=en}}</ref>

India's approach to food self-sufficiency is shaped by [[Green Revolution in India|strategic state policies]] that have historically insulated it from the kind of food scarcity experienced by some African nations that are heavily reliant on food imports.

Data from the Petroleum Planning & Analysis Cell of the Ministry of Oil indicates that India's import dependence for crude oil has escalated to 87.8% in August 2023, an increase from 86.5% in the prior year.<ref name=":14" />

==== Dependence on global export demand ====
Neoliberal reforms have led to a significant increase in exports as a share of the India's GDP. While this has fueled growth in some sectors, it also means that the Indian economy becomes more vulnerable to fluctuations in global market demand. Over-reliance on exports can lead to economic instability if global demand weakens or if there are competitive pressures from other countries. Moreover, this strategy often results in neglecting the domestic market and local production capacities, which can exacerbate economic inequalities and reduce self-sufficiency.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Home |url=https://www.oecd-ilibrary.org/sites/04b94da4-en/index.html?itemId=/content/component/04b94da4-en |access-date=2023-11-06 |website=www.oecd-ilibrary.org |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-08-01 |title=30 Years of Economic Reforms – A Saga of Growing Inequalities |url=https://www.newsclick.in/30-years-economic-reforms-saga-growing-inequalities |access-date=2023-11-06 |website=NewsClick |language=en}}</ref>

India's export demand, influenced by the global market, has seen a contraction in recent times. In April 2023, India's merchandise exports contracted by 12.7%, with imports also seeing a sharp decline due to low demand in the U.S. and EU Markets.

==== Impact on domestic monetary and fiscal policies ====
India's fiscal policies have been criticised by some for prioritizing the demands of foreign investors over the domestic demand and well-being of its citizens. The criticism is rooted in the observation that the Indian government has adopted a regime of fiscal austerity, where it has been reducing its fiscal deficit relative to its GDP by cutting down on revenue expenditure such as welfare, subsidies, and other services. This austerity in revenue expenditure has led to a significant reduction in government spending on welfare, such as health, [[Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005|rural employment]], social assistance, child care centers, [[Midday Meal Scheme|midday meals]], and maternity benefits. As a consequence, the domestic demand is depressed, real wages are falling, and employment situation is dire.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-05-24 |title=Since 2014, the poorest communities are earning less |url=https://indianexpress.com/article/opinion/columns/since-2014-the-poorest-communities-are-earning-less-8625367/ |access-date=2023-11-07 |website=The Indian Express |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-10-07 |title=Who Loses, Who Gains? |url=https://rupeindia.wordpress.com/2023/10/07/who-loses-who-gains/ |access-date=2023-11-07 |website=rupeindia |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Himanshu |date=2023-03-23 |title=Worker incomes in India are still signalling tough circumstances |url=https://www.livemint.com/opinion/columns/worker-incomes-in-india-are-still-signalling-tough-circumstances-11679592796284.html |access-date=2023-11-07 |website=mint |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Narendra Modi's Decade in Power Has Brought a Shrinking Welfare Landscape to India |url=https://thewire.in/economy/narendra-modis-decade-in-power-has-brought-a-shrinking-welfare-landscape-to-india |access-date=2023-11-07 |website=The Wire}}</ref>

[[B. V. R. Subrahmanyam|BVR Subrahmanyam]], the CEO of NITI Aayog said in a speech about cutting funding for Ministry of Women and Child Development “I still remember when we were cutting off … women and child – state subject – 36,000, make it 18,000 crores,” that is 360 billion rupees ($5.8bn) to 180 billion rupees ($2.9bn).<ref name="aljazeera.com">{{Cite web |title=As PM, India's Modi secretly tried to massively cut state funds |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2024/1/18/as-pm-indias-modi-secretly-tried-to-massively-cut-state-funds |access-date=2024-01-18 |website=Al Jazeera |language=en}}</ref>

Additionally, the incomes of informal workers, such as food delivery platform workers, have fallen, and their net incomes have declined significantly after accounting for inflation and fuel costs.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Socio-economic Impact Assessment of Food Delivery Platform Workers |url=https://www.ncaer.org/publication/socio-economic-impact-assessment-of-food-delivery-platform-workers |access-date=2023-11-07 |website=NCAER {{!}} Quality . Relevance . Impact |language=en-US}}</ref>

The government's economic policies, shaped by the desire to attract foreign capital is criticised by some for causing a deterioration in the economic condition of the working class, which potentially leads to a cycle of reduced aggregate demand, further hurting the economy and making it subservient to the interests of foreign capital at the expense of its domestic prosperity.

===== Cutting of state finances =====
In a study conducted in January 2023, researchers from the [[National Institute of Public Finance and Policy]] examined state revenues. Their analysis revealed that in 17 of the 18 states they investigated, the income generated from state-level taxes diminished after implementation of GST compared to the pre-GST era. This decline was observed in terms of the percentage of the gross state domestic product (GSDP).<ref name="aljazeera.com"/> This reduction in revenue leads to states being forced to cut back on spending.

=== Income Inequality ===
The liberalisation of the Indian economy was followed by a large increase in inequality with the income share of the top 10% of the population increasing from 35% in 1991 to 57.1% in 2014. Likewise, the income share of the bottom 50% decreased from 20.1% in 1991 to 13.1% in 2014.<ref>{{Cite web|title=India|url=https://wid.world/country/india/|access-date=2022-01-28|website=WID – World Inequality Database|language=en-US}}</ref> It has also been criticised for decreasing rural living standards, rural employment and an increase in [[Farmer suicides in India|farmer suicides]].<ref name=":10">{{Cite web|date=2017-03-11|title=Please Mind The Gap: Winners and Losers of Neoliberalism in India|url=https://www.e-ir.info/2017/03/11/please-mind-the-gap-winners-and-losers-of-neoliberalism-in-india/|access-date=2022-01-29|website=E-International Relations|language=en-US}}</ref>
Income inequality in India has been a major concern, especially since 2016. The top 10% of the population holds 77% of the total national wealth, with the richest 1% acquiring 73% of the wealth generated in 2017, while the poorest half of the population, about 670 million people, saw only a 1% increase in their wealth.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-09-09 |title=India: extreme inequality in numbers |url=https://www.oxfam.org/en/india-extreme-inequality-numbers |access-date=2023-11-06 |website=Oxfam International |language=en}}</ref>

The annual income of the bottom 20% of households in India experienced a sharp decline of 53% during the pandemic year of 2020-21 compared to their 2015-16 levels, and have yet to bounce back to pre-pandemic levels. In contrast, the top 20% of households saw their annual income increase by 39%. This challenges the neoliberal argument that economic liberalisation benefits all segments to some extent, even if it exacerbates income disparities.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-01-24 |title=Income of poorest fifth plunged 53% in 5 yrs; those at top surged |url=https://indianexpress.com/article/india/income-of-poorest-fifth-plunged-53-in-5-yrs-those-at-top-surged-7738426/ |access-date=2024-01-30 |website=The Indian Express |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=2024-01-25 |title=Incomes up since Covid, but poorest 20% still below FY16 level: Study |url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/india/incomes-up-since-covid-but-poorest-20-still-below-fy16-level-study/articleshow/107124541.cms |access-date=2024-01-30 |work=The Times of India |issn=0971-8257}}</ref>

=== Poverty ===
Poverty continues to persist in India, before the COVID-19 pandemic there were 59 million Indians living below $2 a day and 1,162 million living between $2.01 and $10 a day.<ref name=":11">{{Cite web |last=Kochhar |first=Rakesh |title=In the pandemic, India's middle class shrinks and poverty spreads while China sees smaller changes |url=https://www.pewresearch.org/fact-tank/2021/03/18/in-the-pandemic-indias-middle-class-shrinks-and-poverty-spreads-while-china-sees-smaller-changes/ |access-date=2022-01-31 |website=Pew Research Center |date=18 March 2021 |language=en-US}}</ref>
Low government expenditure on healthcare has resulted in a healthcare quality divide between rich and poor as well as between the rural and urban population.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Private Healthcare in India: Boons and Banes|url=https://www.institutmontaigne.org/en/blog/private-healthcare-india-boons-and-banes|access-date=2022-01-31|website=Institut Montaigne|language=en}}</ref>

==== Decline in consumption ====
The 2017-18 National Sample Survey on consumer expenditure in India which was leaked revealed a worrisome decline in consumer spending, marking the first such drop in 40 years. The survey indicated that the average monthly spending by an Indian fell by 3.7% to Rs 1,446 from Rs 1,501 in 2011–12. In rural areas, the decline was even sharper at 8.8%, although urban spending saw a 2% rise over the same period.<ref name=":13">{{Cite web |title=CEA Has Asked NSC to Release 2017-18 Consumer Spending Data: Report |url=https://thewire.in/economy/cea-nsc-consumer-spending-data |access-date=2023-11-06 |website=The Wire}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-11-15 |title=Consumer Survey 2017-18 junked due to discrepancies; new survey ordered: Govt |url=https://www.businesstoday.in/latest/economy-politics/story/govt-withholds-consumer-spending-report-for-2017-18-on-grounds-of-data-quality-238853-2019-11-15 |access-date=2023-11-06 |website=Business Today |language=en}}</ref>

Despite these concerning findings, the government decided not to release the report, citing "data quality issues" and later scrapped the survey altogether. This action was seen as a rejection of evidence by the government, especially since such surveys are crucial for setting the base year for key macroeconomic data like GDP.<ref name=":13" />
[[File:Producer Support Estimate measured as a percentage of gross farm receipts.jpg|thumb|550x550px|India's Producer Support Estimate consistently registers negative figures, suggesting that the government is more inclined towards taxing or discouraging its agricultural producers, rather than providing them with support or subsidies.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Agricultural policy - Agricultural support - OECD Data |url=http://data.oecd.org/agrpolicy/agricultural-support.htm |access-date=2023-11-09 |website=theOECD |language=en}}</ref>]]

=== Agrarian crisis ===
Neoliberal economic policies have markedly shaped India's agricultural crisis, impacting a vast number of people since more than 70% rely on farming for their livelihood. This situation is intensified by several economic strategies, particularly those shaped by the World Trade Organization (WTO) demands. The WTO urges countries such as India to cut back on agricultural subsidies, which are crucial for sustaining food security and supporting the rural economy.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-03-08 |title=India's new farming laws driven by WTO demands |url=https://www.eco-business.com/news/indias-new-farming-laws-driven-by-wto-demands/ |access-date=2023-11-09 |website=Eco-Business |language=en}}</ref>

Post-1991 economic reforms explicitly rejected the need for institutional transformation in agriculture, leading to a contraction of the role of the Indian state. The state was encouraged to withdraw its protectionist disposition, making way for a free, privatised, and financialised market. The opening up of the markets exposed small farmers to volatile global market forces influenced by heavy subsidies given to agriculture sector in developed countries, against which they were not equipped to compete.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Patnaik |first=Utsa |date=2007 |title=Neoliberalism and Rural Poverty in India |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/4419844 |journal=Economic and Political Weekly |volume=42 |issue=30 |pages=3132–3150 |jstor=4419844 |issn=0012-9976}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Minhaz |first=Ayesha |date=2023-02-23 |title=Neoliberal damage |url=https://frontline.thehindu.com/books/neoliberal-damage-book-review-distress-in-the-fields-indian-agriculture-after-economic-liberalization-edited-by-r-ramakumar/article66507301.ece |access-date=2023-11-09 |website=Frontline |language=en}}</ref>

With the withdrawal of state support and the opening up of agricultural markets, many farmers have had to take loans to keep up with the increased costs of farming, leading to a debt trap for many. The debt trap resulted in a high incidence of farmer suicides. In 2017 alone, 10,655 farmers took their lives due to these pressures.<ref>{{Cite web |title=More than 10,000 farmers, farm hands committed suicide in 2017 |url=https://www.downtoearth.org.in/news/agriculture/more-than-10-000-farmers-farm-hands-committed-suicide-in-2017-68653 |access-date=2023-11-09 |website=www.downtoearth.org.in |date=2 January 2020 |language=en}}</ref>
